title: Thinking
description: Learn how your thinking affects your decisions and actions. Master the Decision Making Tool (DMT), STAC, and belief upgrading to take control of your future.

lessons.title: Decision Making
lessons.description: Learn the Decision Making Tool (DMT) to weigh short- and long-term consequences before making choices.
lessons.videoNote: Watch the Decision Making Tool (DMT) video before starting.

sections.title: What is the DMT?
sections.content: The Decision Making Tool (DMT) helps you weigh out the short and long term positive and negative consequences of different choices. Instead of making decisions based on how you feel in the moment, you learn to think about how your choices will affect your life in the long run (6 months or longer).

sections.title: 1A Decision Making Tool (DMT) Worksheet
sections.content: Use the DMT to weigh out a real decision you are facing right now.

fields.label: What decision are you facing?
fields.placeholder: Describe the specific choice you need to make (e.g., Work legally vs. fast money, cutting off an old friend)...

fields.label: Option 1 (The choice you are considering):
Option 2 (A better or alternative choice):
DMT 4-Box Analysis
Based on your DMT, which option best supports your long-term goals and freedom?
fields.placeholder: Explain your final choice and what sacrifices you may need to make today...

homework.title: 1A Practice Using the DMT
homework.instructions: Apply the Decision Making Tool to a decision you face this week outside of class. Fill in the boxes and decide which choice protects your future.

fields.label: What decision did you face?
Your DMT Analysis
What responsible action did you choose to take?
fields.placeholder: What did you choose and why?

lessons.title: Beliefs
lessons.description: Understand how core beliefs shape your thinking, emotions, and choices.

sections.title: How Beliefs Guide Us
sections.content: Our beliefs are what we accept as true about ourselves, others, and the world. Helpful beliefs push us forward toward success. Harmful or risky beliefs hold us back, make us defensive, or lead to criminal choices.

sections.title: Beliefs Inventory Worksheet
sections.content: Identify core beliefs that have influenced your path.

fields.label: List 3 helpful beliefs that have kept you safe, supported your family, or helped you grow:
fields.placeholder:
1. Hard work pays off in the end
2. My family deserves stability
3. I have the power to change my future

fields.label: List 3 harmful or risky beliefs that led to trouble or legal problems in the past:
fields.placeholder:
1. I have to retaliate if someone disrespects me
2. The system is rigged so why try
3. I need fast money to survive

homework.title: 1B Tracking Your Beliefs
homework.instructions: Notice a moment this week when a belief pushed you toward a reaction. Reflect on whether that belief was helpful or harmful.

fields.label: What was the situation?
What belief came to the surface?
Did that belief help you or make the situation more risky?

lessons.title: Modifying Beliefs
lessons.description: Learn to upgrade old, harmful beliefs into constructive ones that support your life goals.

sections.title: 1D Upgrading Beliefs
sections.content: You cannot change the past, but you can upgrade the beliefs that guide your present choices. Upgrading a belief means taking an old, automatic thought and replacing it with a mature, prosocial truth.

sections.title: 1D Upgrading Beliefs Worksheet
sections.content: List risky beliefs and write replacement beliefs for each one.

fields.label: Risky Beliefs vs. Upgraded Replacement Beliefs

placeholders: e.g. If someone cuts me off, they are disrespecting me
e.g. People make mistakes in traffic; it's not personal and not worth my freedom

homework.title: 1C Practicing Belief Upgrades
homework.instructions: Catch yourself holding onto an old belief this week and write out how you upgraded it in real time.

fields.label: What triggered the old belief?
What was the old belief?
What new, upgraded belief did you replace it with?

lessons.title: Thinking Leads to Action
lessons.description: See how your thoughts directly cause your actions using the STAC tool.

sections.title: The Behavior Chain
sections.content: Events don't make you act — your thinking does. The STAC model shows the chain: Situation -> Thinking -> Action -> Consequences.

sections.title: 1I Situation Thinking Action Consequences (STAC) Worksheet
sections.content: Chart a past situation using STAC to see how your thoughts drove your actions.

fields.label: Situation — What happened? (Be specific, facts only)
fields.placeholder: What was the situation outside your control?

fields.label: Thinking — What thoughts went through your mind right then?
Action — What did you do based on those thoughts?
Consequences — What happened as a result? (Legal, personal, financial)
fields.placeholder: What were the short-term and long-term consequences?

sections.title: 1J Upgraded STAC
sections.content: Now rewrite that same situation with Upgraded Thinking and a New Action.

fields.label: New Upgraded Thinking:
fields.placeholder: What thoughts would have kept you calm and in control?

fields.label: New Responsible Action:
fields.placeholder: What action would you take based on your new thinking?

fields.label: New Positive Consequences:
fields.placeholder: How would your life be better today with that outcome?

homework.title: 1D STAC Real-Life Practice
homework.instructions: Complete a STAC chain for a situation that occurred between classes.

fields.label: 1. Situation:
2. Thinking:
3. Action:
4. Consequences:

lessons.title: Destructive Thinking
lessons.description: Identify patterns of destructive thinking such as blaming, entitlement, and making excuses.

sections.title: 1G Thought Tracker
sections.content: Destructive thinking includes thoughts that justify harmful decisions. The Thought Tracker helps you trace backwards from an intentional action to find the thoughts and feelings that sparked it.

sections.title: 1G Thought Tracker Worksheet
sections.content: Fill in the Action first, then work backwards to find the trigger and thoughts.

fields.label: 1. Action: (A past intentional decision that caused problems)
2. Triggering Situation: (The outside event that set it off)
3. Destructive Thoughts: (List all thoughts you had leading up to the action)
4. Feelings: (What emotions were you experiencing?)

homework.title: 1E Tracking Destructive Thoughts
homework.instructions: Catch a destructive thought this week before it turns into an action. Record it below.

fields.label: What was the destructive thought?
What kind of thinking was it? (Blaming, Entitlement, Excuses, Overreacting)
How did you stop it from turning into an action?
fields.placeholder: What did you do to pause?

lessons.title: Personal Roadmap
lessons.description: Create a personal roadmap to map your long-term goals and stay focused.

sections.title: 1B Personal Timeline & Roadmap
sections.content: Your roadmap connects where you are today to your 1-year and 5-year vision. It acts as your GPS when challenges arise.

sections.title: Roadmap Worksheet
sections.content: Map out your journey step-by-step.

fields.label: 1. Where am I right now in life? (Honest assessment)
2. Where do I want to be 1 year from today?
3. Three concrete action steps I must take in the next 90 days:
4. What obstacles or temptations could derail my progress?
fields.placeholder: Old friends, fast money, transportation, impatience...

fields.label: 5. Who in my support network will keep me accountable?

lessons.title: Upgrade Your Thinking
lessons.description: Put all tools together: recognize risky thoughts and practice full upgrades.

sections.title: 1H Upgrading Thinking Worksheet
sections.content: Fill in the triggering situation and generate 5 new thoughts that support your goals.

fields.label: Triggering Situation:
Risky Thoughts vs. New Goal-Supporting Thoughts

placeholders: e.g. He thinks I'm soft if I don't say something
e.g. Real strength is walking away and staying free for my family

fields.label: New Action based on your upgraded thoughts:

homework.title: 10.h Practice Managing a Setback
homework.instructions: Think about a real-life setback you experienced or imagine one that could realistically happen (transportation breakdown, unexpected delay, work dispute). Answer the 4 questions.

fields.label: 1. What is (or could be) the setback? (Be specific. Something outside your control that affects progress)
2. What risky thoughts or feelings might come up when this happens? (Anger, hopelessness, wanting to give up)
3. Which response shows responsibility and supports your goals?
4. Who could you talk to in your support network about this situation?
fields.placeholder: Name and how they can help...

title: Feelings
description: Learn to recognize, name, and manage difficult emotions. Master warning signs, thought-feeling cycles, and self-control strategies.

lessons.title: Managing Feelings
lessons.description: Learn how feelings drive actions and identify your top risky emotions.

sections.title: The Feeling & Action Cycle
sections.content: Feelings are not right or wrong, but the actions we take when feeling them can change our lives forever. When you learn to catch a feeling before it turns into a reaction, you maintain control.

sections.title: Three Feelings Worksheet
sections.content: Identify the top 3 feelings that have caused you the most problems or trouble in the past.

fields.label: Risky Feeling #1 (e.g., Anger, Disrespect, Boredom, Fear, Embarrassment):
How has Feeling #1 caused trouble for you in the past?
fields.placeholder: Describe past problems caused by this feeling...

fields.label: Risky Feeling #2:
How has Feeling #2 caused trouble for you in the past?
fields.placeholder: Describe past problems caused by this feeling...

fields.label: Risky Feeling #3:
How has Feeling #3 caused trouble for you in the past?
fields.placeholder: Describe past problems caused by this feeling...

homework.title: 2.a Feeling & Action Cycle Homework
homework.instructions: Choose one of your top risky feelings. Identify a possible trigger and what risky action you might take, then write a positive alternative.

fields.label: 1. Triggering Situation:
2. Risky Feeling:
3. What is the risky action you would normally take?
4. What is a responsible action that keeps you safe?

lessons.title: Emotional Goals
lessons.description: Set clear goals for how you want to handle strong feelings before they happen.

sections.title: Setting Emotional Goals
sections.content: Just like wage and career goals, you can set emotional goals. An emotional goal gives your brain a planned response when intense feelings strike.

sections.title: Emotional Goals Worksheet
sections.content: Complete your personal emotional goal statements.

fields.label: When I feel ANGRY, my emotional goal is to:
fields.placeholder: e.g., Take 3 deep breaths, walk into another room, and say nothing for 60 seconds...

fields.label: When I feel DISRESPECTED, my emotional goal is to:
fields.placeholder: e.g., Remind myself that another person's ignorance doesn't define my worth...

fields.label: When I feel OVERWHELMED or FRUSTRATED, my emotional goal is to:
fields.placeholder: e.g., Call my case manager or talk to someone in my support network...

homework.title: 2.b Putting Emotional Goals into Action
homework.instructions: Notice a moment this week when you felt one of your risky emotions. How did you use your emotional goal?

fields.label: What emotion came up?
Did you remember your emotional goal?
What was the outcome?

lessons.title: Knowing Your Warning Signs
lessons.description: Learn to recognize the physical and mental signs in your body before you lose control.

sections.title: Physical Early Warning Signs
sections.content: Your body sends physical signals before an emotional explosion. Catching these early gives you precious seconds to use a self-control tool.

sections.title: Warning Signs Checklist Worksheet
sections.content: Check all physical warning signs you experience when getting angry or upset:

fields.label: Check your personal warning signs:
checklistItems: Urge to hit or break something

fields.label: Which 2 warning signs appear FIRST for you?
fields.placeholder: The very first warning signs I notice are...

homework.title: 2.c Tracking Warning Signs
homework.instructions: Notice your body's physical warning signs during a moment of stress or conflict this week.

fields.label: What was happening?
What exact physical signs did you feel in your body?
What did you do once you recognized the signs?

lessons.title: Knowing Your Feelings
lessons.description: Practice Social Skill #12: Notice sensations, determine the trigger, and name the exact feeling.

sections.title: Social Skill #12: Knowing Your Feelings
sections.content:
Step 1: Pay attention to your physical sensations and body language.
Step 2: Decide what happened to make you feel that way.
Step 3: Name the feeling by saying, 'I feel...'

sections.title: Feelings Vocabulary Worksheet
sections.content: Move beyond just 'mad' or 'good.' Practice naming precise emotions.

fields.label: Scenario 1: You applied for an apartment and the landlord denied your application because of your record. What is the exact feeling?
Scenario 2: A coworker takes credit for work that you did in front of your supervisor. What is the exact feeling?
Why does accurately naming your feeling give you more power than just saying 'I'm mad'?

homework.title: 2.d Noticing and Naming a Feeling
homework.instructions: Between now and our next session, pay attention to a real moment when you experienced an emotion. Follow Social Skill #12.

fields.label: 1. What was the situation? (Describe what happened)
2. What did you notice in your body or physical reactions?
3. What triggered the feeling?
4. What feeling did you identify? ('I felt...')
5. If you were able to name the feeling in the moment, how did that help you?
fields.placeholder: How did naming it help you respond?

lessons.title: Expressing Your Feelings
lessons.description: Master Social Skill #13: Express feelings respectfully using 'I feel...' statements without blowing up or shutting down.

sections.title: Social Skill #13: Expressing Your Feelings
sections.content: Expressing feelings is not about attacking someone or being weak. It is about speaking truth clearly: 'I feel [emotion] when [trigger] because [reason].'

sections.title: Practice 'I Feel' Statements Worksheet
sections.content: Draft 'I Feel' statements for difficult interactions.

fields.label: Practice 1: Someone in your house borrows your tools or clothes without asking.
fields.placeholder: I feel frustrated when you take my tools without asking because I need them for work tomorrow...

fields.label: Practice 2: Your boss changes your shift at the last minute.
fields.placeholder: I feel anxious when shifts change on short notice because my bus schedule is tight...

homework.title: 2.e Expressing a Feeling Homework
homework.instructions: Notice a moment when you felt a strong emotion and expressed it (or could have). Answer the questions.

fields.label: 1. What was the situation?
2. What were you feeling? (Name it clearly)
3. What did you notice in your body?
4. Did you express the feeling to the person involved? How did you say it?
5. Looking back, how well did you follow the steps? What would you do differently?

lessons.title: Understanding Others' Feelings
lessons.description: Practice Social Skill #14: Developing empathy by reading body language, tone, and recognizing what others feel.

sections.title: Social Skill #14: Understanding Others
sections.content: You don't have to agree with someone to understand them. When you can tell when a coworker, boss, or family member is stressed or hurting, you avoid unnecessary friction.

sections.title: Reading Body Language Worksheet
sections.content: Match the body language to the underlying emotion.

fields.label: Body Language Clues & Likely Emotions

placeholders: e.g., Arms crossed, avoiding eye contact, short answers
e.g., Defensive, embarrassed, or guarded

homework.title: 2.f Understanding Someone Else's Feelings
homework.instructions: Notice a moment when you interacted with someone and tried to figure out what they were feeling.

fields.label: 1. What was the situation and who was involved?
2. What did you notice in their body language, tone, or words?
3. What do you think they were feeling?
4. How did you respond to show understanding?

lessons.title: Thought-Feeling Cycle
lessons.description: Break the escalation cycle where negative thoughts fuel intense feelings and vice versa.

sections.title: 1L Thought / Feeling Cycle
sections.content: Thoughts feed feelings, and feelings feed more extreme thoughts. Breaking this cycle early is the key to emotional mastery.

sections.title: Break the Cycle Worksheet
sections.content: Chart out an escalating thought-feeling cycle from your past.

fields.label: 1. Trigger Event:
2. First Thought:
fields.placeholder: The first thought that entered your mind...

fields.label: 3. Feeling Created:
4. Escalating Thought (The thought that threw gasoline on the fire):
fields.placeholder: e.g., They think I'm a joke, I gotta show them...

fields.label: 5. How could you break the cycle at Step 2 with a new thought?
fields.placeholder: Replacement thought to break the loop...

homework.title: 2.g Thought Stopping Homework
homework.instructions: Practice 'Thought Stopping' this week when a stressful or negative thought starts looping.

fields.label: 1. Write down the stressful thought you noticed:
2. What physical or mental cue did you use to stop it? ('STOP', snapping a band, deep breath)
3. What productive thought did you replace it with?

lessons.title: Stop and Think
lessons.description: Master Social Skill #15: The 5-second pause that separates what happens from how you respond.

sections.title: Social Skill #15: Stop & Think
sections.content:
Step 1: Notice your warning signs.
Step 2: Tell yourself to STOP.
Step 3: Take a deep breath and count to 5.
Step 4: Think of your long-term goals.
Step 5: Choose a responsible response.

sections.title: Stop & Think Scenarios Worksheet
sections.content: Walk through how you would use the 5-second pause.

fields.label: Describe a situation where acting immediately in the past caused a catastrophe:
If you had paused for 5 seconds and taken a deep breath in that moment, how would the outcome have been different?
fields.placeholder: How would your life be different today?

lessons.title: Self-Control Strategies: Thinking
lessons.description: Use 4 thinking strategies: Thought Stopping, Visualization, Counting Backwards, and Grounding (5 Senses).

sections.title: 4 Mental Self-Control Strategies
sections.content:
1. Thought Stopping (Firm mental 'STOP')
2. Visualization (Picturing your freedom, your children, or a quiet place)
3. Counting Backwards from 10 or 20
4. Grounding: 5 things you see, 4 you feel, 3 you hear, 2 you smell, 1 you taste.

sections.title: Thinking Strategies Worksheet
sections.content: Select which mental strategies fit you best.

fields.label: Which mental self-control strategy feels most natural for you?
In what specific situation will you test this strategy this week?
fields.placeholder: Describe where you will use it...

homework.title: 2.i Practice Using Thinking Strategies
homework.instructions: Use one thinking strategy to deal with a real-life situation before our next session.

fields.label: 1. What was the stressful situation?
2. Which thinking strategy did you use?
3. How useful was it in calming you down? (1 = Not useful, 5 = Very useful)

lessons.title: Self-Control Strategies: Action
lessons.description: Combine physical action strategies (Breathing, Space, Exercise, Calling Support) with thinking strategies.

sections.title: Combining Thinking & Action
sections.content: Combining a mental strategy with a physical action strategy (e.g. counting backwards WHILE taking deep breaths or stepping outside) is twice as effective as mental strategies alone.

sections.title: Action Strategy Arsenal Worksheet
sections.content: Pick your top physical action self-control tools.

fields.label: Check the action strategies you can realistically use on a job or at home:
checklistItems: Box Breathing (4 sec in, 4 sec hold, 4 sec out, 4 sec hold)
Getting physical space (walking away to restroom or outside)
Going for a brisk walk or workout
Writing your raw thoughts down on paper then ripping it up

homework.title: 2.j Using Thinking & Action Self-Control Strategies
homework.instructions: Practice combining one thinking strategy and one action strategy to deal with a difficult emotion before next class.

fields.label: 1. Did the situation happen in real life or was it a role play?
2. What was the risky feeling?
3. Situation triggering the feeling:
4. Thinking strategy used:
5. Action strategy used:
fields.placeholder: Deep breathing, getting space, calling friend...

fields.label: 6. How useful was the combination? (1 = Not useful, 5 = Very useful)
7. How likely are you to use it again?

title: Thinking Errors
description: Identify and dismantle cognitive distortions: ignoring your past, unrealistic expectations, tunnel vision, should thinking, and blaming.

lessons.title: Ignoring Your Past
lessons.description: Understand why pretending past mistakes never happened guarantees you will repeat them.

sections.title: 1B Looking at Your Past Timeline
sections.content: Ignoring your past doesn't erase it. Examining your history honestly helps you identify dangerous patterns (places, associates, lifestyle habits) so you can build a moat around your future.

sections.title: Past Patterns Worksheet
sections.content: Reflect on patterns across your past arrests or setbacks.

fields.label: When you look back at past charges or setbacks, what common themes stand out? (e.g. Drugs/alcohol, hanging out late, carrying weapons, fast money)
Were you usually alone, or was someone else involved when trouble occurred?
What is ONE concrete thing in your daily life that must be 100% different now to avoid that pattern?

homework.title: 3.a Looking at Your Past Homework
homework.instructions: Answer the questions below based on your life patterns.

fields.label: 1. What is the single biggest pattern that led to trouble in your past?
2. What is an early warning sign that you are slipping back toward that old pattern?

lessons.title: Expectations
lessons.description: Understand how unrealistic expectations set you up for disappointment, anger, and relapse.

sections.title: The Trap of Unrealistic Expectations
sections.content: When we expect everything to happen instantly, or expect other people to treat us perfectly, we set ourselves up for frustration. Reentry takes patience, consistency, and resilience.

sections.title: Expectations vs. Reality Worksheet
sections.content: Examine two expectations that caused frustration.

fields.label: Unrealistic Expectation #1: (e.g. 'I'll get a $30/hr job my first week home')
What was the reality?
Realistic Upgraded Expectation:
fields.placeholder: e.g., 'I will take an entry-level job, build trust for 6 months, and work my way up'...

homework.title: 3.b Unrealistic Expectations Homework
homework.instructions: List an unrealistic expectation you currently have about your goals, relationships, or employment.

fields.label: 1. Unrealistic expectation:
2. Why is this expectation unrealistic?
3. What is a grounded, realistic expectation you can replace it with?

lessons.title: Managing Expectations
lessons.description: Practice Social Skill #10: Managing expectations before they turn into anger.

sections.title: Social Skill #10: Managing Expectations
sections.content:
Step 1: Notice when you are feeling frustrated or let down.
Step 2: Ask yourself, 'Did I have an unrealistic expectation?'
Step 3: Reality check the situation.
Step 4: Adjust your expectations to fit reality.

sections.title: Adjusting Expectations Worksheet
sections.content: Practice adjusting expectations across daily life areas.

fields.label: Expectation Adjustment Table

placeholders: e.g. Probation Officer
e.g. They should trust me immediately
e.g. Trust is earned over time through consistent clean drug screens and being on time

lessons.title: Tunnel Vision
lessons.description: Recognize when you are hyper-focusing on one negative detail and missing the bigger picture.

sections.title: Breaking Out of Tunnel Vision
sections.content: Tunnel vision happens when your attention locks onto a single disrespect, obstacle, or negative thought. You lose sight of your children, your freedom, and your long-term goals.

sections.title: Tunnel Vision Tracker Worksheet
sections.content: Examine a moment where tunnel vision took over.

fields.label: What was the single negative detail you hyper-focused on?
What was the bigger picture you were completely blind to in that moment?
fields.placeholder: My freedom, my family, my job, my future...

fields.label: What mental cue can you use to 'zoom out' next time?
fields.placeholder: e.g. Ask myself: 'Will this matter 1 year from now?'

lessons.title: Personal Risk Factors
lessons.description: Identify the specific triggers, people, places, and situations that put you at highest risk.

sections.title: 1O Personal Risk Factors Worksheet
sections.content: Check all personal risk factors that have contributed to past trouble:

fields.label: Check your personal risk factors:
checklistItems: Negative attitude toward authority / law enforcement
Being used to having fast cash in my pocket
Lack of daily structure / bored with nothing to do
Associating with old friends from past lifestyle
Extreme pride / cannot admit when I'm wrong

fields.label: What are your TOP 3 most dangerous risk factors from this list?

homework.title: 3.e Managing My Top Risk Factor
homework.instructions: Take your #1 risk factor and create a concrete prevention plan.

fields.label: 1. Top Risk Factor:
2. Concrete boundary or rule you will follow to avoid it:
fields.placeholder: e.g., Delete old numbers, never carry more than $40 cash, be home by 9 PM...

lessons.title: Managing Personal Risk Factors
lessons.description: Build an actionable defense plan for each of your high-risk situations.

sections.title: High-Risk Situation Game Plan
sections.content: Create an action plan for when you unexpectedly find yourself in a high-risk situation.

fields.label: If I unexpectedly run into old associates who are engaging in illegal activity, my exit plan is:
fields.placeholder: What exact words will you say? How will you physically leave the scene?

fields.label: Who is the first person you will call immediately after walking away?

lessons.title: Should Thinking
lessons.description: Recognize how demanding that others 'SHOULD' act a certain way creates anger and resentment.

sections.title: The Problem with 'Should'
sections.content: 'Should' thinking is demanding that reality or other people conform to your expectations: 'He SHOULD have known better,' 'They SHOULD respect me.' When they don't, you feel entitled to get angry.

sections.title: Catching Should Thoughts Worksheet
sections.content: Identify 3 'Should' demands you frequently place on others or the world.

fields.label: 'Should' thought #1: (e.g., 'People should always show respect')
How does this thought make you feel when someone doesn't follow it?

lessons.title: Replacing Should Thinking
lessons.description: Replace rigid 'should' demands with flexible preferences ('I would prefer...') and acceptance.

sections.title: Flexible Thinking Table
sections.content: Convert rigid demands into flexible, mature thoughts.

fields.label: Rigid 'Should' Thought vs. Flexible Preference

placeholders: e.g. He SHOULD have kept his mouth shut
e.g. I would prefer if he didn't talk like that, but I can't control him. I can only control me.

lessons.title: Blaming Thinking
lessons.description: Stop blaming others, the system, or circumstances and take full ownership of your choices.

sections.title: Blaming vs. Ownership Worksheet
sections.content: Blaming keeps you powerless. Ownership gives you control.

fields.label: Blaming Thoughts vs. Ownership Thoughts

placeholders: e.g. My friend got me locked up because it was his gun
e.g. I chose to get in that car knowing what he does. I take full responsibility for being there.

homework.title: 3.i Blaming Thinking Homework
homework.instructions: Write down 3 blaming thoughts you caught yourself having, then write 3 new thoughts that focus on personal responsibility.

fields.label: Blaming Thoughts vs. Personal Responsibility

placeholders: e.g. My boss is unfair to me
e.g. If I'm consistently 10 minutes early and do solid work, my boss won't have an issue.

title: Personality
description: Explore personality traits, manage impulsivity with The Domino Effect, and master responding to criticism and authority.

lessons.title: Intro to Personality
lessons.description: Understand the personality traits that shape your behavioral patterns.

sections.title: Personality Traits Assessment Worksheet
sections.content: Check the personality traits that you have exhibited in the past.

fields.label: Check traits that describe your past behavior:
checklistItems: Entitled (believing rules don't apply to me)
Extreme self-focus (only looking out for myself)
Quick to anger / aggressive when challenged

fields.label: Which ONE trait do you most want to change during your time in Turn90?
fields.placeholder: The trait I want to reshape is...

lessons.title: Personality & Beliefs
lessons.description: Examine how core beliefs fuel troublesome personality traits.

sections.title: Beliefs Behind the Trait Worksheet
sections.content: What beliefs drive your selected personality trait?

fields.label: What beliefs keep this personality trait alive?
fields.placeholder: e.g., If my trait is Entitlement, the belief is 'I shouldn't have to start at the bottom'...

lessons.title: Personality & New Beliefs
lessons.description: Construct new foundational beliefs to build the person you want to become.

sections.title: New Identity Beliefs Worksheet
sections.content: Create 3 new beliefs that will reshape your character.

fields.label: 3 New Identity Beliefs:
fields.placeholder:
1. Real respect is earned through consistency
2. Patience creates lasting wealth
3. Admitting mistakes shows maturity

lessons.title: Impulsivity
lessons.description: Use Tool 1P: The Domino Effect to connect impulsive actions to cascading consequences.

sections.title: 1P The Domino Effect Worksheet
sections.content: Trace how a single impulsive action knocks over consecutive dominos into disaster.

fields.label: Domino 1 — Impulsive Action: (e.g. Taking a drink, cursing out a manager, staying out late)
Domino 2 — Immediate Consequence: (What happens right away?)
fields.placeholder: Fired from job, failed drug screen, argument...

fields.label: Domino 3 — Risky Reaction: (How you react to Domino 2)
fields.placeholder: Give up, go back to old associates, hang out on corner...

fields.label: Domino 4 — Final Severe Consequence: (The final crash)
fields.placeholder: Probation violation, prison sentence, lost custody...

homework.title: 4.d The Domino Effect Homework
homework.instructions: Identify an impulsive action you were tempted to take this week. Chart what the dominos would have looked like if you had not stopped yourself.

fields.label: Domino Chain (Action -> Consequence -> Reaction -> Final Result):

lessons.title: Entitlement
lessons.description: Dismantle entitlement and replace it with a willingness to earn your success.

sections.title: Entitlement Call & Response Worksheet
sections.content: Replace entitled thoughts with humble, realistic truths.

fields.label: Entitled Thinking vs. Earned Mindset

placeholders: e.g. I have experience, I shouldn't have to sweep floors
e.g. Sweeping floors with a great attitude proves I'm reliable and opens the door for promotion.

lessons.title: Extreme Self-Focus
lessons.description: Learn how extreme self-focus damages relationships and isolates you.

lessons.title: Responding to Criticism
lessons.description: Practice Social Skill: Listening to correction or criticism without getting defensive or angry.

sections.title: 4 Steps to Handling Criticism
sections.content:
Step 1: Look at the person and listen without interrupting.
Step 2: Stay calm — don't argue or roll your eyes.
Step 3: Decide if there is truth in what they are saying.
Step 4: Acknowledge the point or calmly explain your side later.

lessons.title: Deciding to Say No

sections.title: Social Skill: Saying No
sections.content:
Step 1: Look at the person.
Step 2: Use a clear, firm tone of voice.
Step 3: Say 'No' or 'No, I can't do that.'
Step 4: Give a short, honest reason if appropriate.
Step 5: Suggest a safe alternative or walk away.

lessons.title: Assertive Communication

sections.title: The Assertive Formula
sections.content:
Passive: You don't speak up and build resentment.
Aggressive: You attack and violate others.
Assertive: You speak up clearly, calmly, and respectfully: 'I feel [emotion] when [event] because [reason]. I would like [request].'
